questions.topic: C99 Standard — Implicit return 0 in main()
questions.q: What will happen in C99/C11 standard if main() reaches the closing brace } without an explicit return statement?
questions.hint: Recall C99 innovation regarding main function execution reaching the end.
options: The compiler will automatically insert return 0 (EXIT_SUCCESS)
A random value (garbage from register) will be returned, as this is Undefined Behavior
A compilation error will occur — return in main is strictly required
The function will return -1
explanations: Correct! Starting from the C99 standard, if control reaches the end of `main()` without encountering a `return`, the compiler implicitly returns `0` (`EXIT_SUCCESS`).
Incorrect. Random garbage was returned in C89/C90 standard, but starting with C99, returning 0 is guaranteed.
Incorrect. The code will compile successfully without errors.
Incorrect. By default, 0 is returned upon successful completion.

questions.q: What is the argv[argc] element guaranteed to be equal to when passing command-line arguments to int main(int argc, char *argv[])?
questions.hint: Does the C standard allow iterating through the argv array via pointers up to a null terminator?
options: NULL pointer
Name of the program itself
Undefined value (out of bounds array access)
Pointer to an empty string ""
explanations: Correct! By the C standard, `argv[argc]` is always equal to `NULL`. This allows iterating through arguments with a `while (*argv != NULL)` loop without explicitly using `argc`.
Incorrect. The program name is equal to `argv[0]`.
Incorrect. This is not out of bounds: the size of `argv` is `argc + 1` elements.
Incorrect. This is specifically a null pointer `NULL`, not a pointer to an empty string.

questions.q: Why is the void main() signature non-standard for a standard (hosted) C execution environment?
questions.hint: How does the operating system learn about the program's exit status?
options: The C standard requires int type; the void main() signature is implementation-defined and can lead to an incorrect return code in the OS
Because void functions are forbidden in C
Because main() with void cannot accept argc and argv arguments
The void main() signature will become standard only starting from C23
explanations: Correct! In a hosted environment, the C standard requires return type `int`. The operating system expects to receive an exit code via the return register. Using `void main()` can lead to undefined behavior when reading the call status.
Incorrect. Functions with `void` type are fully supported by C.
Incorrect. Receiving command-line arguments does not depend directly on the return type.
Incorrect. In C23, `int main()` remains standard.

questions.topic: GCC/Clang Extensions — Executing Code Before main()
questions.q: Which function attribute in GCC/Clang compilers can force a function to execute BEFORE control is passed to main()?
questions.hint: Recall the term for initialization constructs.
options: __attribute__((constructor))
__attribute__((before_main))
__attribute__((startup))
__attribute__((init))
explanations: Correct! Functions with `__attribute__((constructor))` are placed in the `.init_array` section and automatically called by the CRT runtime before entering `main()`.
Incorrect. The `before_main` attribute does not exist.
Incorrect. Keyword `startup` is not used for this attribute.
Incorrect. The attribute is named `constructor`.

questions.q: What does the third (non-standard, but widely supported) parameter in main(int argc, char *argv[], char *envp[]) contain?
questions.hint: Think about process environment variables (PATH, HOME, etc.).
options: Array of strings with process Environment Variables
Array of OS kernel arguments
Pointers to open file descriptors
List of loaded dynamic libraries
explanations: Correct! In signature `int main(int argc, char *argv[], char *envp[])`, parameter `envp` represents a `NULL`-terminated array of strings of form `KEY=VALUE`, containing environment variables.
Incorrect. Kernel arguments are passed via regular `argv` when launching init/systemd.
Incorrect. File descriptors are tracked by the OS and are not passed to `main` parameters.
Incorrect. Dynamic libraries are loaded by system linker and do not reside in `envp`.

questions.topic: Standard Restrictions — inline Qualifier for main()
questions.q: Is applying the inline qualifier to main() function allowed by the C standard?
questions.hint: Does inlining make sense for the entry point of a program?
options: No, the C standard explicitly forbids declaring main() function as inline
Yes, it is common practice to speed up program startup
Allowed only when argc and argv arguments are omitted
Allowed only in C23
explanations: Correct! By the C standard, function `main()` cannot be declared with `inline` qualifier, because it is an external entry point of the program and inlining it is meaningless.
Incorrect. The prohibition is explicitly written in the standard.
Incorrect. Presence of arguments does not affect this prohibition.
Incorrect. In C23 this prohibition persists.

questions.q: What does using macros EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE from <stdlib.h> instead of numbers 0 and 1 guarantee when returning from main()?
questions.hint: Is code 0 always indicative of success on all target platforms and OSes?
options: Cross-platform compatibility — macros expand into correct exit codes for a specific OS
Protection against memory leaks upon exiting main()
Speeding up process termination
Automatic call to fflush() for all stdout streams
explanations: Correct! Although on POSIX and Windows `EXIT_SUCCESS` is 0, on some non-standard OSes successful exit code may differ. Using macros from `<stdlib.h>` guarantees portability.
Incorrect. `EXIT_SUCCESS` does not affect memory cleanup.
Incorrect. Process termination speed is identical.
Incorrect. Flushing stream buffers is done by standard on any normal `return` from `main` or call to `exit()`.

questions.q: What is a C execution environment called (e.g. for OS kernel or microcontrollers) where presence of main() function and standard libraries is not required?
questions.hint: As opposed to Hosted Environment.
options: Freestanding Environment
Hosted Environment
Sandbox Environment
Kernel Environment
explanations: Correct! In a Freestanding environment, program executes without an operating system. The entry point is defined by developer/compiler (e.g., `Reset_Handler` or `_start`) and is not required to be named `main()`.
Incorrect. Hosted Environment specifically requires `main()` and the entire C standard library.
Incorrect. Sandbox is execution isolation, not a C standard term.
Incorrect. Kernel Environment is a general concept, but C standard uses term Freestanding.

questions.q: Is it safe to overwrite characters inside argv[i] strings (e.g., argv[1][0] = 'a')?
questions.hint: Are strings in argv constant literals?
options: Yes, strings and the argv array itself are guaranteed to be modifiable within passed length
No, this will cause Segfault because argv points to Read-Only memory
Forbidden by C standard and leads to UB
Only argv[0] can be modified
explanations: Correct! C standard guarantees that `argv` parameters are passed as modifiable character arrays. Modifying them is legal (often used to hide passwords from process list `ps`).
Incorrect. Strings in `argv` are not placed in read-only memory segment.
Incorrect. This behavior is allowed by C standard.
Incorrect. All elements from `argv[0]` to `argv[argc-1]` can be modified.

questions.topic: Program Termination — exit() vs return in main()
questions.q: What is the main difference between calling exit(0) and calling return 0 inside main() itself?
questions.hint: Are local destructors/stack cleaners called on exit()?
options: exit(0) terminates process without unwinding main() stack frame, while return 0 correctly closes main() stack
exit(0) does not call functions registered via atexit()
return 0 does not flush stdout/stderr buffers
There is no difference at all
explanations: Correct! When calling `exit(0)`, local variables of `main()` do not leave scope naturally (their cleanup attributes are not called) because stack is not unwound. With `return 0`, standard function return occurs.
Incorrect. Both `exit()` and `return` from `main()` equally call functions registered via `atexit()`.
Incorrect. Both methods automatically flush and close file streams.
Incorrect. Difference in unwinding stack frame of `main()` itself is significant for automatic resources.

questions.q: What is actually the true Entry Point for an ELF executable file in Linux prior to calling main()?
questions.hint: Think about the C Runtime (CRT) function that prepares stack and arguments.
options: Service function _start provided by CRT library
Function main() is called directly by Linux kernel
Special macro __init_main()
Function init() from standard library
explanations: Correct! Entry point of an ELF file is symbol `_start`, provided by CRT (C Runtime) startup code. This function sets up environment, stack, `argc`/`argv` arguments, and only then calls `main()`.
Incorrect. Linux kernel transfers control to `_start`, not directly to `main()`.
Incorrect. Macro `__init_main()` does not exist in C/CRT standard.
Incorrect. `init()` is not standard CRT entry point.

questions.q: Does the C standard guarantee that argv[0] always contains file name of launched program?
questions.hint: Can calling process (e.g. via execve) pass something else in argv[0]?
options: No, parent process can pass an arbitrary string or even NULL in argv[0]
Yes, OS always automatically overwrites argv[0] with real file name
Yes, this is a strict C standard requirement for all operating systems
No, argv[0] is always empty, and program name resides in argv[1]
explanations: Correct! Standard defines that `argv[0]` represents program name *if available*. However, when calling system functions like `execve()`, calling process can pass any string or `NULL` as first argument.
Incorrect. OS passes exactly the `argv` array constructed by calling process.
Incorrect. Standard allows cases where program name is unavailable.
Incorrect. By convention `argv[0]` is used to pass name, but this is not 100% guaranteed.

questions.topic: Scope — Static Variables in main() Recursion
questions.q: How does a local variable with static modifier inside main() behave during recursive call to main()?
questions.hint: Does static variable depend on current stack frame?
options: Retains its value between calls because it is placed in global data segment, not on stack
Recreated on stack on each recursive call
Causes compilation error when attempting to combine static and main()
Automatically resets to 0 on each new call
explanations: Correct! Variables with `static` qualifier have static storage duration and are placed in data segment (BSS or Data). They are initialized once before program startup and retain value between recursive `main()` calls.
Incorrect. Only `auto` variables are placed on stack.
Incorrect. Static variables are allowed inside any function, including `main()`.
Incorrect. Initialization occurs only once at startup.

questions.topic: Function Pointers — Taking Address of main() Function
questions.q: Is taking address of main() function (e.g. &main) valid in C standard?
questions.hint: Recall if status of main() in C differs from C++.
options: Yes, in C you can take address of main and pass it to function pointer (unlike C++)
No, taking address of main is strictly forbidden in all C standards
Allowed only in C89
Allowed only when static attribute is present
explanations: Correct! In C, `main()` is a regular function. You can take its address `&main` and call via pointer. In C++, taking address of `main` or calling `main` from program is forbidden.
Incorrect. In C this is a completely legal operation.
Incorrect. Allowed in all C standards.
Incorrect. `main()` cannot be declared `static` in hosted environment.

questions.q: At what point is a function marked with __attribute__((destructor)) attribute called?
questions.hint: Analogous to constructor attribute, but upon program termination.
options: After exiting main() or calling exit(), prior to final process termination
Immediately before entering main()
Only upon occurrence of fatal error (Segmentation Fault)
Only when calling abort()
explanations: Correct! Functions with `destructor` attribute are entered into special `.fini_array` section and automatically executed prior to program unloading after return from `main()` or call to `exit()`.
Incorrect. For code before `main()`, `__attribute__((constructor))` is used.
Incorrect. On Segfault crash CRT destructors may not have time to execute.
Incorrect. `abort()` terminates process abnormally without running exit handlers.

questions.topic: C11 Standard — Quick Termination via quick_exit()
questions.q: How does quick_exit() function distinguish its termination process from regular exit() when called from main()?
questions.hint: Are registered atexit() functions called and file buffers flushed?
options: quick_exit() does NOT call atexit() functions and does NOT flush file buffers, replacing them with at_quick_exit()
quick_exit() executes 2 times faster by disabling optimizations
quick_exit() calls only compiler destructors
There is no difference between them
explanations: Correct! Function `quick_exit()` (C11) is designed for 'fast' exit: it does NOT run `atexit()` handlers and does NOT flush open `stdio` streams. Instead, it calls only functions registered via `at_quick_exit()`.
Incorrect. Speed is achieved by skipping cleanup steps, not disabling optimizations.
Incorrect. It works with `at_quick_exit` list.
Incorrect. Behavior fundamentally differs regarding invocation of registered cleanups.

questions.topic: main Parameters — Modifying Pointers in argv Array
questions.q: Is reassigning pointers of argv array itself (e.g., argv[1] = "new_str") permitted?
questions.hint: Distinguish between modifying characters in string and replacing elements of pointer array itself.
options: Yes, argv array consists of regular char* pointers, which can be reassigned
No, argv array is const char * const argv[] and protected against changes
This leads to compilation error
Only argv[0] can be modified
explanations: Correct! Argument type is `char *argv[]`. Pointer array itself and strings they point to are not declared `const`. You can reassign element `argv[i] = "other_string"`.
Incorrect. `const` qualifiers are absent from standard `main` signature.
Incorrect. Assignment operation is completely valid from type system perspective.
Incorrect. All elements of pointer array can be modified.

questions.topic: Memory Management — Huge Arrays on Stack in main()
questions.q: What problem will declaring array char buf[16 * 1024 * 1024] as an automatic local variable inside main() lead to?
questions.hint: Recall standard thread stack size in popular OSes (typically 1 to 8 MB).
options: Stack Overflow and abnormal program termination
Memory will automatically redirect to Heap
Compiler will issue build error
Program will run without any issues
explanations: Correct! Variable `buf` will be allocated on stack. On most OSes (Linux/Windows), default stack size is 1 to 8 MB. Attempting to allocate 16 MB will cause Stack Overflow when `main()` is called.
Incorrect. Automatic transfer of local arrays from stack to heap does not exist in C.
Incorrect. If size is known at compile time, compiler silently generates stack pointer offset.
Incorrect. Upon accessing memory beyond stack limit, crash (Segmentation Fault) occurs.

questions.q: Are functions registered via atexit() called when invoking _Exit(code) (or _exit) function?
questions.hint: Think about purpose of low-level instant process termination functions.
options: No, _Exit() terminates process immediately without calling atexit() functions or cleaning up stdio
Yes, _Exit() is a complete synonym of exit()
Yes, but only if exit code is 0
Only GCC destructors are called
explanations: Correct! Function `_Exit()` (C99) / `_exit()` (POSIX) performs instant program exit at kernel level without calling functions from `atexit()` or `at_quick_exit()` and without flushing `stdio` buffers.
Incorrect. `exit()` performs full high-level CRT cleanup, unlike `_Exit()`.
Incorrect. Exit code does not affect skipping cleanup procedures.
Incorrect. `_Exit()` immediately makes system process exit call.

questions.q: Is it required to declare prototype of main() function at start of file prior to its definition?
questions.hint: Is a header file or prototype required for main function?
options: No, main() is entry point and does not require prior prototype declaration
Yes, this is mandatory C standard requirement
Yes, main() prototype is contained in <stdio.h>
Yes, if main() is called recursively
explanations: Correct! Function `main()` does not require prototype declaration. System header files do not contain it either — compiler knows existence of entry point by default.
Incorrect. C standard does not require prototype for `main()`.
Incorrect. `<stdio.h>` and other standard headers do not have `main()` prototype.
Incorrect. For `main()` recursion prototype is also unneeded if function definition is at top level.

questions.q: What does Function Prototype represent in C?
questions.hint: Think how to inform compiler about function existence before its body is written.
options: Function declaration without its body, informing compiler of name, return type, and function parameters
Function code compiled into separate library
Variable storing result of function work
Special preprocessor macro for calling functions
explanations: Correct! Prototype (e.g. `int add(int, int);`) informs compiler of function signature, allowing it to be called before full definition in code and performing argument type checking.
Incorrect. Prototype is only syntactic declaration in code, not binary file.
Incorrect. Prototype describes function itself, not result.
Incorrect. Prototypes are part of C syntax, not preprocessor.

questions.q: What does using void as return type of a function mean (e.g. void print_msg(void))?
questions.hint: Is returning something via return necessary from such function?
options: Function returns no value to calling code
Function returns random integer
Function returns NULL pointer
Function can return value of absolutely any type
explanations: Correct! Keyword `void` as return type value means function performs actions (side effects), but passes back no result.
Incorrect. `void` guarantees complete absence of return value.
Incorrect. For returning null pointer type `void*` would be used, not `void`.
Incorrect. `void` denotes emptiness/absence of type, not universal type.

questions.q: How are basic variables (int, float, char) passed to function parameters in C by default?
questions.hint: Does original variable in main change if corresponding parameter inside function is modified?
options: By value (local copy of variable is created inside function)
By reference (modifying parameter inside function changes original variable)
By pointer automatically
Through global memory area
explanations: Correct! In C arguments are always passed by value. Function receives copies of passed data, so parameter changes inside function do not affect calling code variables.
Incorrect. Passing by reference (like `&` in C++) does not exist in pure C.
Incorrect. To pass value by pointer pointer syntax `*` must be used explicitly.
Incorrect. Parameters are allocated in local stack frame.

questions.q: What is difference between terms 'parameter' and 'argument' of a function?
questions.hint: What is written in function declaration vs passed during actual call?
options: Parameters are variables in function declaration, while arguments are specific values passed during call
They are complete synonyms, no syntactic or terminological difference exists between them
Parameters are used only in main(), while arguments — in all other functions
Parameters are data types, while arguments are variable names
explanations: Correct! In declaration `void foo(int x)`, variable `x` is formal parameter. In call `foo(5)`, number `5` is actual argument.
Incorrect. Although often confused in speech, in standards and C terminology these are distinct concepts.
Incorrect. Both terms apply to absolutely any function.
Incorrect. Parameter includes both type and variable name.

questions.q: What happens to a regular local variable created inside a function upon exiting that function?
questions.hint: Where are function local variables stored?
options: Variable is destroyed, and memory allocated for it on stack is freed
Variable retains its value until next function call
Variable automatically becomes global
Variable moves to dynamic memory (heap)
explanations: Correct! Regular (automatic) local variables live only during execution of function block. Upon return from function, stack frame is cleared, and variable ceases to exist.
Incorrect. For variable to retain value between calls, it must be declared `static`.
Incorrect. Scope of local variable is limited to function body.
Incorrect. In heap memory is allocated only manually via `malloc/calloc`.

questions.q: Which statement is used to terminate function execution and return result to call point?
questions.hint: This keyword is present in all functions returning a result.
options: return
yield
break
exit
explanations: Correct! Statement `return` terminates current function execution and passes expression value to calling code.
Incorrect. `yield` is used in other languages (e.g. Python/C#) for generators.
Incorrect. `break` is used to exit loops and `switch` constructs.
Incorrect. `exit()` terminates whole program completely, rather than returning value from single function.

questions.q: What is called a recursive function in programming?
questions.hint: What does recursive function do inside its body?
options: A function that calls itself
A function that has no parameters
A function executing in an infinite loop
A function working without return statement
explanations: Correct! Recursion is a technique where function calls itself (directly or via other functions) to solve subtask.
Incorrect. Presence or absence of parameters does not make function recursive.
Incorrect. Recursion must have base case to stop, otherwise it causes stack overflow.
Incorrect. To return values from recursion `return` statement is actively used.

questions.q: How to allow function to modify value of variable located in calling main() function?
questions.hint: What needs to be passed in parameter instead of regular value?
options: Pass address of variable (pointer) and dereference it inside function
Use keyword ref before argument
Simply change variable name to parameter name
In C it is impossible to modify variable from another function
explanations: Correct! Passing address of variable `&x` to pointer `int *p`, function gains direct access to memory of original variable and can modify it via dereference `*p = val`.
Incorrect. Keyword `ref` is used in C#, in C it does not exist.
Incorrect. Variable names in different scopes are not linked in any way.
Incorrect. Using pointers is standard way to modify calling function data.

questions.topic: Errors — Missing return in Non-void Function
questions.q: What will happen if in function with int type do_math(void) return is omitted and attempt is made to use its result?
questions.hint: Does C standard guarantee any specific default value for regular functions?
options: Undefined Behavior (UB) occurs, and program receives random garbage from register
Compiler will automatically always return number 0
Program will print error and close correctly
Result automatically becomes equal to NULL
explanations: Correct! Unlike `main()`, for all other functions missing `return` with declared return type leads to Undefined Behavior when attempting to read call result.
Incorrect. Automatic `return 0` is guaranteed by C99 standard only for `main()` function.
Incorrect. Runtime protection against missing `return` is usually absent.
Incorrect. NULL is used for pointers, not for `int` type.

questions.q: Which of the following lines is correct syntax for calling function int sum(int a, int b)?
questions.hint: Do data types need to be specified when calling a function?
options: int result = sum(5, 10);
int result = sum(int a = 5, int b = 10);
int result = call sum(5, 10);
int result = sum[5, 10];
explanations: Correct! When calling function only expressions/values inside parentheses `sum(5, 10)` are passed, specifying parameter types again is unnecessary.
Incorrect. Repeatedly specifying types `int a = ...` on call is syntax error.
Incorrect. Keyword `call` is not used in C.
Incorrect. For calling functions parentheses `()` are used, not square brackets `[]`.
